newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Senate passes contentious tax bill.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Senate passes contentious tax bill.

text.p: The Philippine Senate on Thursday passed a contentious tax bill, scrapping the present ad valorem system on both beer and cigarettes and replacing it with specific excise taxes.
President Fidel Ramos had been pushing hard for this bill since this would be simpler to enforce and would help plug loopholes which allowed large-scale tax evasion.
The bill was passed two months after the House of Representatives passed its own version which sought to impose a specific or ad valorem tax system, whichever is higher.
The lower house version was criticised by the government saying it would fail to accomplish the planned tax reforms.
Since the two house of the legislature have different versions to the bill, it will be sent to a bicameral conference committee which will begin meetings next week.

"I'm confident I can convince them (the Lower House) to accept the Senate version. I think (the Senate) rates are very reasonable. In fact, we considered sectoral and economic circumstances of consumers," Senator Juan Ponce-Enrile, chairman of the ways and means committee said.

Finance Undersecretary Milwida Guevarra had earlier said "the issue is more of social justice and equity in our capacity to put (in place) a reform that is correct, that will be simple for us and rid itself of tax avoidance opportunities."

According to the Senate, its proposed rates on cigarettes would earn additional revenues of "a little less than four billion pesos" in the first year of implementation versus the House version which would generate 3.38 billion pesos.
Taxes on beer would have an additional 1.2 billion pesos in the first year if the Senate version was followed compared with 520 million pesos from the House proposal.

The Senate would impose a four-tiered specific tax rate on cigarettes. Enrile's formula is broken down as follows: one peso per pack for low-priced cigarettes (below five pesos per pack when other taxes are netted out); five pesos for medium-priced (5.0 to 6.50 pesos); eight pesos for high-priced (6.50 to ten pesos) and 12 pesos for cigarettes priced more than ten pesos.

In the House bill, a tax rate of 1.50 pesos would be placed on every existing brand of cigarette with a retail price, net of other taxes, not exceeding six pesos. A tax rate of four and six pesos per pack would be imposed on other cigarettes.
The House also required a tax equivalent to 55 percent, 45 and 20 percent of the retail price of cigarettes should these come out higher than the computation on the specific tax rates.

The proposed Senate taxes on beer are as follows: 6.30 pesos per litre with net retail prices below 14.50 pesos; 9.30 pesos per litre of brands with net retail prices of 14.50 to 22.00 pesos; and 12.30 pesos per litre of brands with retail prices of more than 22 pesos per litre.

The House version would have a six-peso tax rate per litre of beer for those with a retail prices below 17 pesos; and nine pesos per litre if the retail price exceeds 17 pesos for the first two years of effectivity of the law.
The House also recommended a tax equivalent to 35 percent of the retail price of beer if it comes out to be higher than the specfic tax rate.
